sections.summary: An unusually weighted salutation in which Paul denies any human source for his commission and attaches to the greeting a clause defining Christ's work as a voluntary self-giving that rescues the hearers out of the present evil age according to God's will.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading identifies exaireo as the exodus verb of the Greek scriptures and reads the clause as announcing a rescue enacted by God's own initiative and located in his purpose rather than in an emergency measure, which is language of divine action on the hearers' behalf rather than of their performance. But the reading also stresses that the rescue is out of an age the recipients are still standing in -- something has happened to them that has not yet happened to the world around them -- so the clause states the ground of their deliverance without saying anything about whether it can be forfeited.
key_phrases: who gave himself for our sins
so that he might deliver us out of the present evil age
according to the will of our God and Father

sections.summary: Paul replaces the customary thanksgiving with a formula of rebuke, states that the Galatians are in the act of transferring away from the God who called them in grace toward something that is not a second gospel at all, and twice pronounces anathema on anyone preaching a message contrary to what they received.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading makes two points that bear directly on the question. First, what they are leaving is described as a person, not a doctrine -- apo tou kalesantos hymas, 'from the one who called you,' a participle that refers to God throughout Paul's usage -- so people who were called in grace are described as walking away from the caller. Second, metatithesthe is present tense and means changing sides, so the movement is under way and not complete: the letter is written to people the writer believes can still turn back, which presupposes both that the departure is real and that its outcome is not yet settled. The section is nonetheless arguing about the gospel's integrity and the standing of those who preach it, not systematically about whether a believer's standing can be lost, so the conditionality is carried in the premise rather than asserted as the point.
key_phrases: you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ
not that there is another one

sections.summary: Paul states the thesis of the autobiography -- that his gospel is not patterned on human thinking, was not received by transmitted tradition and was not taught to him, but came through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

sections.section_title: The Former Life, and the Call
sections.summary: Paul describes his former life of zealous violence against the assembly in the vocabulary of Ioudaismos, ancestral tradition and zeal, and then describes God setting him apart from the womb, calling him by grace and revealing his Son in him so that he might announce him among the nations, after which he consulted no one and did not go to Jerusalem.
sections.relevance: The womb-language of 1:15-16 is conventionally enlisted, alongside Romans 8:29-30 and Jeremiah 1:5, to argue for an unconditional individual election to salvation fixed before birth and therefore unlosable. The neutral reading shows the sentence is built from Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1, 6 and has the form of a prophetic commissioning rather than a conversion: nothing here describes guilt relieved, beliefs exchanged or a religion left, and the purpose clause states what the setting-apart was for -- preaching among the nations. This is election to an assignment, and the neutral reading's own conclusion is that the Gentile mission is the content of the call rather than a later development. Nothing in the passage addresses whether the standing of a believer before God is secure; the section is functioning as evidence that Paul's message did not come from Jerusalem.
key_phrases: set me apart from my mother's womb
to reveal his Son in me
so that I might preach him among the Gentiles

sections.section_title: Jerusalem at Last, and Then Away Again
sections.summary: Paul establishes by chronology and by oath that his first Jerusalem visit came three years after his call, lasted fifteen days and involved two people, that he remained personally unknown to the Judean assemblies, and that those assemblies glorified God over the report that their former persecutor now preached the faith he once tried to destroy.
